title: The Sunlight Soap Story

paragraphs.text: The first bars of Sunlight soap rolled off the Lever Brothers production line in January 1886 at their factory in England. The Lever brothers – William and James – were respectively the seventh and eighth in a family of ten, and the only boys. Their father was a grocer, and the youngsters were apprenticed to the family business, where William soon showed a good business sense and entrepreneurial ability. By the time he was in his mid-twenties he was virtually running the firm, and hungry for greater challenges. He found them in soap.

Soap was becoming popular in the late 19th century and Lever, while admitting he was not knowledgeable about soap itself, realised that a good product at a reasonable price could be a winner. His original idea was to buy soap from a manufacturer then package and market it with his own brand, and he set about seeing what might be on offer. One soap was outstanding; it foamed up easily, it was sweet-scented, and it met all his criteria except one – it was too expensive, because its manufacturers raised the price when they realised Lever wanted an exclusive deal. William decided to buy the recipe instead, for a small sum of money, and manufacture the soap himself. The main ingredients were copra oil from coconuts, and tallow, a hard substance made from animal fat.

When the ingredients were boiled in a vat with a strong alkaline solution, soap was formed, with glycerine as a valuable by-product. Rather trickier was the correct proportion of preservatives and scents that were then added to the soap. Sodium silicate was used by most manufacturers as a 'filler', but Lever preferred not to use it at all in his new brand he called Sunlight soap. Without it, he could advertise his product as 'pure', which made for great advertising.

With some financial help from his father, William was able to buy a soap factory, complete with a manager/chemist and mechanical soap boiler. Initially, the factory turned out 450 tons of soap a week; by the end of the year that had increased to 3,000 tons, and by December 1888, the weekly output was 14,000 tons.

As William expanded the soap business, his philosophy was that all men could improve themselves if they were given a fair chance. He was dismayed by the slums that were so much a part of the Victorian industrial scene, and he saw no reason why workers should not benefit from the profits created by his business each year. And so Lever constructed 'Port Sunlight' – a village, complete with open spaces and public buildings, and numerous leisure facilities. At a time when planning regulations allowed more than forty houses to the acre, Lever would permit no more than seven. He also looked after his workers in other ways – there were staff outings, and no child's birthday passed unnoticed at Port Sunlight.

William Lever wanted the whole world to use Sunlight soap, and he very nearly succeeded. Before the end of the 19th century, his product could be found in nearly every European country, in India, and in many other countries from China to Argentina. The packaging surrounding the soap was produced in no fewer than thirty languages to appeal to customers around the world.

Headquarters for the Australasian division were in Sydney, and every opportunity was seized to advertise his soap in this new area. In New Zealand and Australia, the soap was even promoted on the backs of postage stamps. New Zealand and Australia produced large quantities of tallow, and were close to the copra-producing islands of the South Pacific, so it seemed logical to extend the soap-making operations to Australia. Lever Brothers (New Zealand) Limited was incorporated in May 1919, and the new factory began producing soap, by the simple process of running the liquid soap base on to the floor and raking soda ash into it.

Sunlight did have its rivals, of course, but a good product and great advertising gave Sunlight by far the biggest share of the market. A rapidly-increasing standard of living and the ready availability of the washing machine meant that powders were replacing bar soaps in many homes. And so, in the early 21st century, Sunlight soap production ended at the New Zealand plant. New Zealand then began to import Sunlight soap from Australia. Although other products are now available, it remains a popular brand.
